title: TB6-17419
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) and substitute a decision with its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD with a differently constituted panel. The Appellant has submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in Section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1 and requests an oral hearing be held pursuant to Section 110(6) of the IRPA.
Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he fears the Tehrik-e-Taliban ("TTP" or "Taliban") if he were to return to Pakistan due to his tribal affiliation and anti-Taliban political opinion. The Appellant alleges his tribe formed a XXXX XXXX XXXX consisting of about XXXX XXXX people to monitor the Taliban and report back to the government. The Appellant alleges he was a XXXX XXXX XXXX of about XXXX men in the XXXX XXXX XXXX.

In 2011, the Appellant alleges the Taliban left pamphlets in front of his house demanding he stop his activities on the XXXX XXXX. In 2012 the Appellant and his family returned to their home in the village of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX However the area was controlled by the group XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who demanded protection money from the Appellant to protect them from the Taliban. The Appellant alleges he was beaten twice by this group for resisting to pay the protection money. In XXXX of 2013 there was intense fighting between the Taliban and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He and his family fled their homes and went to the XXXX area. Subsequently, they went back to XXXX. The Taliban came looking for him and he decided to move his family to the XXXX area of XXXX.

On XXXX XXXX, 2014 the Appellant left Pakistan with the assistance of an agent, travelling through several countries before entering the United States (US) on XXXX XXXX, 2014 where he was detained for over one year. He made an asylum claim in the US which was refused in XXXX of 2015. On XXXX XXXX, 2016 the Appellant made a refugee claim at the port of entry in XXXX, Manitoba.

The Appellant's hearing for refugee protection was on June 6, 2016. In a decision of November 10, 2016, the RPD rejected the Appellant's claim finding that the Appellant was not credible. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in drawing its credibility findings and in its treatment of the documentary evidence.

The RAD finds that the Federal Court of Appeal decision, in Huruglica,2 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal.

The RAD concludes from its statutory analysis that, with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD's decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred. ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

As provided for in s. 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and refugee claimant. Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.
The Appellant has submitted three news articles3 as proposed new evidence with the Appellant's Record.
The Appellant submit that the proposed new evidence meets the test of s. 110(4) of the IRPA because it arose after the refugee claims.

The RAD's analysis of the admissibility of the proposed new evidence must begin first with the test set out in s. 110(4). While the RAD agrees with the Appellant that further analysis of the evidence is required before the RAD can accept the proposed new evidence, the analysis as set out in Raza4 is not entirely appropriate for the purpose of assessing evidence submitted to the RAD. In this regard, the RAD is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Singh.5
Accordingly, the RAD has adapted the analysis in Raza6 to the assessment of evidence submitted to the RAD.

In assessing whether the proposed new evidence meets the statutory provisions of s. 110(4), the RAD considered the following: a) First, did the evidence arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim? Here, the RAD may consider whether the evidence is capable of proving the current state of affairs in the country of feared persecution, or an event that occurred or a circumstance that arose after the rejection of the refugee claim.7 b) The RAD will consider not only the date on which the document came into existence, but the timing of the event or circumstance which the document seeks to prove.8 For example, an affidavit or newspaper article may have been created after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, but the information in the document may be several years old, and the RAD may therefore find that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claim, despite the date of the document. c) It is important to note here that s. 110(4) does not contemplate whether the evidence arose after the RPD hearing, but rather after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. Where a document arose after the hearing but before the rejection of the refugee claim, it is necessary for the RAD to consider whether the Appellant could have presented the document to the RPD by way of a post-hearing submission. d) If the evidence is capable of proving an event that occurred or circumstances that arose after the RPD hearing, then the evidence must be considered, and the RAD will proceed to assess the credibility, relevance, and materiality of the document.9 e) Second, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, it must consider the next factor in s. 110(4). If the evidence is capable of proving only an event that occurred or circumstances that arose prior to the rejection, has the Appellant established that the evidence was not reasonably available for presentation to the RPD before it rejected the claim,10 or that it proves a fact that was unknown to him at the time of the hearing?11 If so, the RAD will proceed to assess the newness, credibility and relevance of the evidence. f) Third, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, and that it was reasonably available at the time of the rejection, it must consider the final part of the s. 110(4) test: could the Appellant reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence prior to the rejection of the refugee claim? If so, the evidence need not be considered.12 If the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to present the evidence to the RPD, the RAD will proceed to assess the newness, credibility, and relevance of the evidence. g) If the proposed new evidence meets the tests set out in the statutory requirements and in Raza,13 the evidence will be admitted as evidence in the appeal. The relevance of the evidence will be considered in the context of the assessment made under section 110(6) of the IRPA.

The Appellant has submitted three news articles as new evidence in this appeal. a. An article from DAWN.com, "Five Terrorists Shot Dead in Encounter", published December 19, 201614 b. An article from TNN.com, "Waquas trained in Taliban jihad camps", published December 15, 2016.15 c. An article published in the Nation newspaper, "ISIS men among 7 held in Multan, Sialkot raids", published December 14, 2016.16

The Appellant submits the articles were all published since the rejection of his refugee claim and that they are all relevant in that they reference terrorism related activity in the proposed IFA location of Lahore, Hyderabad or Multan. The RAD finds these documents meet the basic requirement of section 110(4) as they all arose following the rejection of the Appellant's claim for refugee protection. The RAD further finds the articles do meet the requirements of Raza.17 , in that they are new and they do address terrorist activities in the proposed IFA location.
The RAD will admit these documents as new evidence in this appeal.

According to Section 110(6), upon which the Appellant relies, the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The RAD has reviewed the documents submitted as new evidence in this appeal. The RAD notes: * Article "a", "Five Terrorists Shot Dead in Encounter", details that the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) of the police in Lahore killed five suspected terrorists belonging to the TTP. The article further noted that the police recovered a number of weapons and they continue to pursue three or four accomplices who escaped. The Appellant submits that the article supports the notion that Taliban terrorists are active in Lahore. The RAD notes that while the article indicates that a Taliban faction may be present in Lahore, it confirms that the police in Lahore are taking an active role in attempting to counteract and subdue terrorist activities, and they were successful in this instance. The RAD further finds that the article does not provide any evidence to support the appellant's argument that the Taliban have the ability to locate him in the proposed IFA location. The RAD finds it does not provide persuasive evidence to support this central element of the Appellant's claim. * Article "b", "Waquas trained in Taliban jihad camps", describes that a highly sought individual, was tried along with four others and convicted of a 2013, bombing of a shopping district in Hyderabad. The appellant submits that the conviction of a man with ties to the Taliban is relevant to his argument that Hyderabad is not safe as a potential IFA location. The RAD notes that the article does not state that these individuals are members of the Taliban. The RAD additionally notes that there is no persuasive evidence to support the concept that these individuals had any ability to communicate directly with the Taliban. The RAD further finds that the article confirms a successful arrest and prosecution of a wanted terrorist by the authorities in Pakistan. The RAD finds this article does not provide evidence that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. * Article "c", "ISIS men among 7 held in Multan, Sialkot raids", details that the provincial CTD arrested seven terrorists, in two separate investigations, three of whom were alleged to be members of ISIS. The article notes the militants were plotting gun and bomb attacks on shrines, religious processions and government installations. The article carries on to describe a second arrest of four individuals who were associated with the TTP, who had come to Multan to launch attacks on sensitive installations and law enforcement. The RAD notes the article does not indicate the Taliban are active in Multan, but it clearly states the Taliban members traveled to Multan to carry out their attack. The RAD additionally notes that the terrorist attacks described in this article are not targeted at a single individual, but appear to be designed to focus on disruptive techniques inflicting harm on any or all who may be present in the immediate area. The RAD finds that any Pakistani citizen could be at risk of this form of terrorist attack. Further to this the RAD finds the article describes two successful investigations and arrest of terrorists by the Pakistani authorities. The RAD finds this article does not provide evidence that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The RAD notes that although new evidence has been admitted in this appeal it must proceed without a hearing. The RAD finds the documents provide insufficient persuasive evidence to support the Appellant's allegation that the Taliban in Pakistan will be able to seek him out in the IFA location. At its best they establish that the authorities in Pakistan are actively attempting to detect and counteract the efforts of terrorist groups. Accordingly the evidence lacks the materiality to justify either allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim, and, as such, it does not meet the requirements of 110(6). Each of the requirements in 110(6)(a) through (c) have to be met, and in this case the requirement in 110(6)(b and c) are not met. As such, the RAD has no discretion to hold a hearing.
As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the RPD's record, and his application for an oral hearing is denied. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Psychotherapist Report

The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to take into consideration the findings of the "XXXXt" that the Appellant suffers from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX anxiety disorder and a XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The RAD finds that the RPD considered the report of Ms. XXXX. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the RAD has conducted its own assessment the XXXXreport18. Although, referred to by the Appellant in his pleadings as a "XXXX", the RAD notes that report's author, Ms. XXXX is not a medical doctor, psychiatrist, or psychologist. Rather, she is a registered XXXX "specializing in the assessment and treatment of serious disorders of thought, cognition, mood, emotional regulation, perception, and memory." Her assessments are based on "in-depth clinical and psychodynamic interviews, typically extending for 60 minutes."19

Although Ms. XXXX is not a medical doctor, psychiatrist, or psychologist, she appears to communicate a diagnosis finding that the Appellant is exhibiting symptoms consistent with XXXX as well as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The RAD notes that section 27 of the Regulated Health Professionals Act, S.O. 1991, Chapter 18 describes the communication of a diagnosis as a "controlled act," not to be performed unless the communicator is so authorized by a health profession Act, or unless the action has been delegated by a person who is so authorized. It does not appear that Ms. XXXX meets either qualification. The controlled act of diagnosis, at S.27(2)(1), is communicating to the individual or his personal representative a diagnosis identifying a disease or disorder as the cause of symptoms of the individual in circumstances in which it is reasonably foreseeable that the individual or his personal representative will rely on the diagnosis.

Ms. XXXX letter clearly sets out to communicate a diagnosis, to be relied upon in these proceedings. The RAD notes that contravention of the Regulated Health Professionals Act by a psychotherapist is considered professional misconduct.20 This assessment deserves little weight, as its author is neither a doctor nor a psychologist and therefore not qualified to make or communicate a diagnosis.21 Although she indicates that the appellant could benefit from a plan of medical and therapeutic care which would include, medication, proper counselling and strategies, there is no evidence that any such plan was put in place.

Further, Ms. XXXX went well beyond the scope of even a psychological or psychiatric report when she went on to advocate for the Appellant to remain in Canada. For all these reasons, the RAD gives this report no weight. Did the RPD Err in its Assessment of the Appellant's IFA?

The RAD finds, after its own review and assessment of the evidence, that the determinative issue in this appeal is IFA. The RPD found that the Appellant has a reasonable IFA in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.
The Appellant submits that the RPD assessment of his IFA is based in disregard for the documentary evidence provided in the National Documentation Package (NDP) and post-hearing submissions.

In assessing an IFA, the RAD must apply a two-pronged test cited in Rasaratnam:22 1) the Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. 2) moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellant has an IFA. The burden of proof rests with the Appellant to show that he does not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose taking into account the Appellant's identity. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The Appellant cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.23 First Prong The Documentary Evidence

The RAD has considered if the Appellant will face risk in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore due to his profile as an individual being sought by the TTP in Pakistan. The RAD notes that the documentary evidence indicates the TTP in Pakistan does not operate as a unified, integrated organization with a solitary hierarchical structure. This information comes from a July 2014, Response to Information Request prepared by the IRB research directorate, which describes the TTP as follows: Sources describe Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) [also known as Tehrik-e Taliban, Pakistani Taliban, Pakistan Taliban, Tehreek-e-Taliban, Tehrik-e-Taliban and Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan] as "an alliance of militant groups" (US 2014); "a coalition" of militant and extremist groups (The Guardian 9 June 2014a; CFR 18 Nov. 2013); and "an umbrella organization" uniting militant groups (The New York Times 2 Nov. 2013; TRAC n.d.). According to sources, TTP was formed when various militias coalesced in 2007 (US 2014; CFR 18 Nov. 2013; The New York Times 2 Nov. 2013). According to sources, TTP is based in the tribal areas along the border between Pakistan and Afghanistan (The Guardian 9 June 2014a; The New York Times 2 Nov. 2013; US 30 May 2013). Sources indicate that members of the group originate from all seven tribal agencies in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), as well as many districts of the northwest province of Khyber Pakhtunkhawa (ibid.; SATP [2014]). The New York Times specifies that TTP's headquarters is in North and South Waziristan {The New York Times 2 Nov. 2013). However, sources note that TTP has also expanded into other areas of the country {SATP [2014]; CNN 17 Oct. 2012). According to CNN, "they maintain loose factions spread out as far as Punjab province" (ibid.}. The Guardian describes TTP as "fractious" and "fracture-prone" (The Guardian 9 June 2014a}. CNN explains that "[a]s a result of its beginnings, Tehrik-i-Taliban are not a unified fighting force," adding that the militant groups which comprise TTP "control different regions within the tribal area and often have different agendas and political objectives. The factions don't always speak with one voice" (CNN 17 Oct. 2012).24

The RAD further notes that the documentation states that "their ability to deploy suicide bombers makes them a threat throughout Pakistan".25 Given the documentary evidence on the operation of the Pakistani Taliban, it does not indicate that a specific individual would be targeted if they are not a high profile person. The documents make reference to bombs being used for terrorism and the organization being capable of deploying suicide bombers, however personal targeting in these attacks is not something that features prominently in the documentary evidence. The RAD notes the Appellant has testified that he was a member of the peace committee where he lived. The RAD has reviewed the Appellant's testimony in respect of his activities and it finds on a balance of probabilities that the Appellant did not occupy a high profile position. The RAD further finds this is confirmed through he Appellant's ability to reside in the XXXX area of Peshawar for three to four months without any problems with the Taliban. Therefore, the RAD finds the Appellant's it highly unlikely the Appellant would be personally targeted by the Taliban in other areas in Pakistan.

Country documentation from the United Kingdom Home Office states: The Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) provided an assessment, published November 2013, with regard to internal relocation in Pakistan, stating: 'Because of Pakistan's size and diversity, internal relocation offers a degree of anonymity and the opportunity for victims to seek refuge from discrimination or violence. In most cases, there are options available for members of most ethnic and religious minorities to be able to relocate to areas of relative safety elsewhere in Pakistan. In particular, many large urban centres are home to mixed ethnic and religious communities and offer greater opportunities for employment, access to services and a greater degree of state protection than other areas. In practice, internal relocation is most successful when these conditions exist, but is limited mostly by a lack of financial resources and in some cases due to debts owed to landowners or money lenders.'26

The UNHCR Guidelines for Assessing the International Protection Needs of Members of Religious Minorities from Pakistan: Given the wide geographic reach of some armed militant groups, a viable IFA will generally not be available to individuals at risk of being targeted by such groups. The operational capacity of certain militant groups, such as the Lashkar-e-Jhangvi and Sipah-e-Sahaba Pakistan, extends far beyond FATA or the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province as evidenced by high-profile attacks, such as suicide bombings, countrywide, particularly in urban centres. Furthermore, some non-State agents of persecution, such as local powerbrokers, organized criminal elements, as well as armed militant groups, reportedly have links to or are closely associated with influential actors in the local and central administration, law enforcement and/or judiciary. As a result, they often operate with impunity and their reach may extend beyond the area(s) under their immediate control.27

The RAD in assessing this documentation finds that it is necessary to consider the nature of the group targeting the Appellant in respect of the availability of an IFA in Pakistan. The RAD has considered the statements in the UNHCR document which clearly states certain militant groups, such as the Lashkar-e-Jhangvi and Sipah-e-Sahaba Pakistan have a reach beyond their physical point of origin. The RAD has considered that this document does not specifically reference the TTP. The RAD notes that the IRB Response to Information Request (RIR) discussed previously specifically notes that the TTP are a fractious group and they do not appear to have the ability to track individuals.

The RAD notes that the RPD found that there was no documentary evidence to support that the TTP members in XXXX, (Peshawar region) who targeted the Appellant would learn of the Appellant's presence in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore. The RAD has reviewed the evidence and finds: * The evidence before the RPD and the RAD establishes the TTP in Pakistan does not operate as a unified, integrated organization that operates within a solitary hierarchical structure. * The limited documentary evidence that indicates the TTP have been active in Lahore. The RPD found that the British Home Office references an Australian government source saying that 'the current security situation in Islamabad and Lahore is relatively free from politically-motivated, terrorist and sectarian violence.'28 * The evidence that the Taliban has carried out attacks against state actors and members of religious minorities or others it perceives to be in opposition to its goals, which have taken place mainly in the region previously known as the FATA, close to the Appellant's home in Peshawar region, and in other regions distant from the proposed IFA locations.29 * The proposed IFA in Hyderabad (a city of over 3 million people), Multan (a city of 1.3 million) or Lahore, (a city of 8.741 million people), which all qualify as a "large urban center" that would provide a "degree of anonymity" as stated in the U.K. Home Office document. * That considering the geographic size of Pakistan, the large number of ports of entry to the country, and the vast population of Lahore, the it would take a significantly coordinated, networked and organized entity to target the Appellant in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore. The documentary evidence does not support the notion that the TTP has that organizational ability.

The RAD has reviewed the available documentary evidence as well as the audio recording of the hearing. The RAD notes that in order to target the Appellant in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore, the TTP would be required to: 1.) Learn the Appellant has returned to Pakistan; 2.) Learn the Appellant has relocated to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore; and 3.) Determine the whereabouts of the Appellant in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that if an organization was of sufficient strength and reach to be able to learn of a person's return to Pakistan or their presence in any city in Pakistan, there would be objective country condition evidence to support this.

The RAD has reviewed the submissions of the Appellant, the available documentary evidence, and finds that as much as it accepts that the Appellant was targeted by individuals who identified themselves as members of the TTP, there is not sufficient credible evidence to establish that they have the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellant's return to Pakistan upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellant's movements within Pakistan.
The RAD finds the documentary evidence does not support that the TTP has that ability in Pakistan. The RAD supports the findings of the RPD in this instance. The Appellant's Profile

The RAD notes the Appellant has testified that he was a member of the XXXX XXXX where he lived. The RAD has considered the Appellant's submission that the RPD misstated the Appellant's risk due to his profile as a sub-leader of volunteers (as described in his BOC narrative). The RAD has reviewed the Appellant's testimony in respect of his activities and it has previously found that the Appellant did not occupy a high profile position in his committee. The RAD further considered that the Appellant had resided in the XXXX area of XXXX for three to four months without the Taliban seeking him out. Therefore, the RAD finds the Appellant's it highly unlikely the Appellant would be personally targeted by the Taliban in other areas in Pakistan.

The Appellant argues that the RPD ignored the documentary evidence of the risk to the Appellant as a member of his local peace committee. Notwithstanding the allegation of error, the RAD has reviewed the specific documentary evidence addressed by the Appellant30 as well as the IRB country documents to conduct its own assessment. The RAD notes the UK Home Office document describes the profile of individuals sought by the Taliban and the principle areas where this occurs: Primary targets include political and/or tribal leaders, security forces and minority religious groups. However, ordinary Pakistanis, including students and those perceived to be opposing the Taliban and other militant groups or not following sharia law, have also been subjected to violence by these groups. The risk will be highest in areas where those armed anti-government groups are operating or have control. (RAD's emphasis) Those main areas are: * Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (formerly known as North West Frontier Province), * The semi-autonomous Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) that have a strong Taliban presence; and * Baluchistan, where separatists are seeking greater political autonomy and control over local mineral resources. The Pakistani Taliban and other militant groups do however have reach outside of those areas.

The RAD finds the documents addressed by the Appellant describe attacks within the Peshawar region during a period between March 2011 and May 2013. The RAD in reviewing the articles notes that at least two of the episodes involved roadside IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices) which were not specifically targeting one individual. Another individual described in one of the articles as being targeted, had a long history of conflict with the Taliban and was linked to the deaths of nine Taliban militants in 2009. The RAD further notes an additional article indicates the Peace Committee in that area is being disbanded because of the risk involved to its participants. The RAD also finds that the articles allege the Taliban are responsible for these events, but a number of the articles clearly note that no specific organization has claimed responsibility for the events.

The RAD finds the evidence does confirm the risk to individuals, especially those of a high profile, during the time period of the articles, in the Peshawar area. The RAD having reviewed all of the documentary evidence available finds there is no persuasive evidence that the Taliban have conducted any operations associated with the targeting of XXXX XXXX outside of the immediate Peshawar region.

The RAD notes the Appellant has also addressed a number of articles31 in the Memorandum that it alleges the RPD ignored in the Appellant's post hearing submissions. The RAD has reviewed these articles and finds they address non-targeted suicide attacks in locations in Multan and Lahore allegedly associated with factions of the Taliban.

The RAD finds it of interest that 4 of 5 articles confirmed the action of the police or the authorities in arresting, detaining or stopping Taliban members involved in various terrorism related activities. A sixth article references the authorities intercepting a telephone call and attempting to protect a jail superintendent in Hyderabad from Taliban militants. The RAD finds these articles indicate limited non-targeted activity by Taliban factions in the areas of the IFA, but more importantly the RAD finds they demonstrate that Pakistani authorities have attempted with some success to address terrorism related issues in these areas.

The RAD further finds that this evidence does not indicate that the Taliban has targeted specific individuals with a profile such as the Appellant, nor does it confirm that the Taliban the willingness or ability to search for the Appellant outside of XXXX in the Peshawar region.

The RAD has reviewed the submissions of the Appellant, the available documentary evidence, and finds that as much as the Appellant may have been targeted by individuals in his home village who identified themselves as members of the TTP, there is not sufficient credible evidence to establish that they have the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellant's return to Pakistan upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellant's movements within Pakistan.
The RAD has previously discussed that the documentary evidence does not support that the TTP has that ability in Pakistan. The RAD agrees with the findings of the RPD in this instance.

The RAD notes that no persuasive evidence was advanced to confirm that the TTP in XXXX have searched for the Appellant in Pakistan since he left the area in XXXX 2014. As well the RAD notes no evidence was presented to the RPD or RAD to suggest that the alleged agent of persecution has the willingness or ability to search for the Appellant elsewhere in the country. The RAD finds that the Appellant has not provided sufficient persuasive evidence to corroborate his speculation that the individuals from the TTP in XXXX who sent letters to him and sought him, have the ability to locate him elsewhere in Pakistan. As such, the RAD finds the problem faced by the Appellant is limited and local in nature. The RAD finds the Appellant's argument must fail. Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore as an IFA

The RAD has previously discussed that the proposed IFA in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore are centres which qualify as a "large urban centers". The RAD notes the RPD questioned the Appellant about his ability to reside in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore and he testified that his only concern was that there is no safe place in Pakistan. The RPD asked the Appellant how the Taliban would be able to find him in those areas. He testified that the Taliban could track him down because they have a wide network including connections in government and the police.

The RAD notes the Appellant provided no credible testimony or evidence as to how this might occur. The RAD has considered that a review of the RPD country condition documents and the Appellant's documentary evidence do not corroborate the Appellant's allegations. The RAD finds upon its review of the evidence there is not a serious possibility that the Appellant would face persecution at the hands of members of the TTP in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore. The Second Prong

The RAD notes the Appellant has a grade eight education, he is an experienced international traveller and has resided in a number of locations. He has testified to being familiar with asylum procedures in the United States and Canada. In addition he has a diploma in XXXX XXXX and speaks Urdu, Pashto and some English. The RAD finds that the Appellant has not adduced any evidence to confirm that there are any circumstances or conditions which would make Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore an unreasonable IFA.
The RAD does not find the Appellant's argument sufficient to justify his failure to attempt relocation within his home country.

The test for reasonableness is whether it would be unduly harsh to expect the Appellant to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking status abroad as per Thirunavukkarasu.32 This requires an evaluation of the conditions in the IFA as well as the Appellant or similarly situated persons. Thirunavukkarasu sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances. The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable.33 Additionally, it is not enough for the Appellant to say that he or she does not like the weather there, or that he or she has no friends or relatives there, or that he or she may not be able to find suitable work.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that there are no serious social, economic or other barriers to the Appellant relocating to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore. The RAD finds after a full assessment of the evidence that the Appellant would not suffer from undue hardship in relocating to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

The RAD, therefore, agrees with the finding of the RPD and finds that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellant, for him to seek refuge there. In Summary

Accordingly, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not satisfied his burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.
